reason: Anita Young (E001) is a full-time Payroll Specialist per HR's database — the authoritative source for employment status — and this is corroborated by IT, Finance, Compliance, and Facilities notes. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, so under policy full-time employees whose role owns the system may have admin. The requested level is admin, which is at the maximum, so grant admin. (Note: the Security note lists E001 as a contractor with basic training; however, HR is the system of record for employment type and five of six notes confirm full-time.)

- Recommendation: admin
- Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, so admin is permitted for full-time employees.

- Security training: basic (looked up in own database)
- Role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up; same value as other notes)
- Recommendation: read
- Comment: Security DB shows E001 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors can receive read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds maximum, so grant read.

So there's a conflict: HR and others say full-time, but Security says contractor with basic training (looked up in own database).

The Security agent looked up employment type in their own database. HR said full-time (looked up in own database). The other agents relied on HR note.

Which is correct? The policy: full-time employees up to write, admin only if role owns system. Contractors: read, or write with advanced training, never admin.

The key conflict is employment type. HR (note 1) looked up in own database: full_time. Security (note 6) looked up in own database: contractor, with basic security training.

Hmm. Who to trust? The notes say HR looked up employment type in own database before writing. Security also looked up employment type in own database. They disagree.
